name: pymol
why: Molecular visualization is real science you can run at home, though it is a well-known tool.

brief.what_it_is: PyMOL is a molecular visualization system for rendering and inspecting 3D molecular structures such as proteins and other biomolecules. The homepage describes it as a user-sponsored system on an open-source foundation, maintained and distributed by Schrodinger. The open-source repository is the foundation, and the full commercial product (called 'Incentive PyMOL' in the repo README) adds maintenance and support. The pages I read do not spell out the inputs and outputs in detail, so treat that part as general knowledge rather than something the README confirms. The homepage's sponsorship and fellowship pages suggest it is funded by license purchases.
brief.why_it_exists: The open-source page frames it as a way to make the source freely available while funding development through commercial licenses: 'Open source enables open science.' It credits the original author, Warren L. DeLano, with that vision.

commands_seen.context: Homepage install option: installs the PyMOL bundle from the Schrodinger Anaconda channel.
INSTALL file: clean build and installation from the open-source source tree.
INSTALL file: recommended for developers, enables incremental builds and C++ unit tests.
INSTALL file: how to launch PyMOL after building from source (also $PYTHONUSERBASE/bin/pymol).

brief.install_notes: Prebuilt bundles are offered for Windows (EXE installer or ZIP), macOS (DMG, Apple Silicon; Intel Macs use older versions per the page), and Linux (TAR.BZ2). The current bundle on the homepage includes Python 3.10. Getting the current version needs a 'Buy License' or, for existing users, 'Download License File'. The open-source build from source needs a C++17 compiler (gcc 8+), CMake 3.13+, Python 3.9+, pip with the build submodule, OpenGL, GLEW, libpng, freetype, glm, and other optional libraries (PyQt/PySide, GLUT, libxml2, msgpack-c, mmtf-cpp, netcdf, openvr, catch2). Build options include --pymol-path, --no-launcher, and environment variables such as PREFIX_PATH and CXX. The INSTALL file links to a Linux install wiki page. The brew caveat for this package says movie generation needs 'brew install ffmpeg'; that comes from the package metadata, not the README.
brief.standout: It is a commercial product that publishes most of its source under a BSD-like license, with the open-source foundation funded by license purchases. That is an unusual model for a scientific visualization tool, and it is the framing the homepage leads with.
brief.status: Maintained, per the homepage. It says 'Version 3.1.9 - Updated October 7th 2026' and lists a 2.6.2 LTS line dated February 5th 2025. The GitHub README shows a CI badge but no release date, and I did not check commit history, so the date claim is only what the homepage states.
brief.caveats: The full product requires a commercial license for current versions; the open-source code is a separate build. Intel Macs and older versions are on separate download pages. Building from source has many dependencies and optional features, and the install depends on a C++17 toolchain and OpenGL. Movie export needs ffmpeg installed separately. The homepage bundles Python 3.10, while the 2.6 LTS bundles Python 3.11. I could not confirm the release date or check the license file beyond the README's 'BSD-like' statement.
quotes: PyMOL is a commercial product, but we make most of its source code freely available under a permissive license.
Published under a BSD-like license, see LICENSE.

judge.reason: PyMOL opens an accessible, hands-on way to inspect and manipulate the 3D structures of proteins and other molecules, a worthwhile scientific rabbit hole beyond ordinary visualization.

entry.title: PyMOL
entry.tldr: A molecular viewer for spinning proteins and other biomolecules in 3D, built on open-source code that commercial licenses pay for.
entry.deeper_look:
PyMOL renders and inspects 3D molecular structures such as proteins and other biomolecules. The homepage describes it as a user-sponsored system on an open-source foundation, maintained and distributed by Schrodinger. The brief does not spell out inputs and outputs, so the usual picture applies: you load a structure, rotate it, and change how it is drawn.

The odd part is how it is funded. The open-source repository holds most of the source under a BSD-like license, while the full commercial product, called 'Incentive PyMOL' in the repo README, adds maintenance and support. License purchases pay for development. The homepage credits the original author, Warren L. DeLano, with that vision, and puts it this way: "Open source enables open science."

The door it opens is structural biology. Proteins are shapes, and much of what they do follows from those shapes. A viewer like this lets you look at one and see why a drug fits a pocket or why a fold holds together. The name hints at Python, and the install pulls in python and numpy, but the brief does not describe the scripting side, so look there yourself.
entry.install:
brew install pymol
# To generate movies, also run: brew install ffmpeg
# Needs OpenGL and a desktop session; the formula pulls in PyQt for the GUI.

Prints the command-line options the launcher accepts.

entry.whats_unique: It is a commercial product whose source is mostly published under a permissive license, with license sales funding the open code. That is an unusual model for scientific visualization software.
entry.caveats: Current commercial versions need a paid license, the open-source build is separate, and the brew formula's own licensing and version may differ from the homepage bundles.
